analysis.one_liner: Repeals the 2010 health care law in full, restoring the rules it replaced.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 2 Republican cosponsors, was referred to eight House committees, sent to two subcommittees, and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would wipe out the Affordable Care Act and the health care and student loan law passed in 2010, erasing them as if they had never been enacted and putting the old rules back in place [S2][S3]. That would end the law's protections for people buying insurance — like the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions — and the tax credits that help pay for coverage. It would also roll back changes that shifted federal student loans from banks to direct government lending, and would repeal the extra Medicare taxes the law placed on the highest incomes [S2].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main gains would go to concentrated interests: high-earning households would no longer pay the ACA's extra Medicare taxes, banks would get back the business of issuing federally subsidized student loans, and insurers and drug makers would be freed of the law's requirements — including drug discounts for seniors and the individual mandate that guaranteed insurers a steady base of customers. Some people who disliked the law's coverage requirements would also get what they wanted.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the entire Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act and the Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010, effective as if each had never been enacted, and restores the provisions of law they changed [S2][S3].

Ending the health law would repeal its tax increases, which fell substantially on high-income households through Medicare taxes, and undo the law's shift of federal student lending away from private banks [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary families would bear the cost: people with pre-existing conditions would again be denied or priced out of coverage, the tax credits that help pay premiums would disappear, seniors would lose the requirement that drug makers discount their Medicare medicine, and young adults would lose guaranteed coverage on a parent's plan.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the law as-is, with no replacement, would strip away coverage protections and subsidies that tens of millions of Americans had begun using, from the pre-existing-conditions ban to premium tax credits.

Even a supporter would have to acknowledge that repeal restores the old insurance market's ability to deny coverage for pre-existing conditions and reimposes the senior 'donut hole' drug costs that the 2010 law had begun closing.

Repeal would also unwind the student loan overhaul that eliminated payments to private lenders for originating federal student loans, restoring a bank-subsidized lending channel at federal expense [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered no replacement for the law it repealed — it was a straight repeal, effective as if the 2010 laws had never existed. The benefits it delivered ran mostly to high earners and industries shedding regulation or subsidy, while the costs fell on insurance consumers who would have lost protections and financial help. An honest supporter would have to concede that repealing first, without a replacement in hand, left nothing standing between millions of people and the old market's exclusions.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee: the bill was referred to eight House committees, then to two subcommittees, and no committee or full chamber ever voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve King (R-IA) introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the opening day of the 112th Congress, with Rep. Michele Bachmann listed as an original supporter [S3][S1].
It was referred the same day to eight House committees, including Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce [S5][S1].
It was later referred to subcommittees on Health and on Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, and no committee ever reported it or scheduled a vote [S5].
The bill died at the end of the 112th Congress without ever coming to a floor vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ordinary people kept the law's protections and subsidies intact — nothing changed for anyone. Insurers also kept the guaranteed customer base the individual mandate provided, high earners kept paying the ACA's Medicare taxes, and private banks stayed out of originating federal student loans. The status quo, which the bill existed to overturn, simply held.

for.name: Rep. Steve King
for.role: House Republican from Iowa; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Affordable Care Act and the 2010 health care and student loan law on the first day of the 112th Congress [S3][S1].

for.name: Rep. Michele Bachmann
for.role: House Republican from Minnesota; original supporter
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original supporter at introduction [S3].

sides.party_line_note: No roll call ever occurred, but every listed sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, and the bill died in a House controlled by the sponsor's own party without reaching the floor.

industries.note: Repeal would free insurers from the law's consumer rules — no denial for pre-existing conditions, rating limits, and medical-loss requirements — but would also end the individual mandate that guaranteed them a steady base of paying customers. In this bill the deregulated version of the industry's interest runs against the insurance consumer's.
The 2010 law's Medicare tax increases fell on the highest incomes; full repeal would erase them. That tax cut is paid for by removing coverage help and protections for the broader public.
The Health Care and Education Reconciliation Act ended payments to banks for originating federal student loans; repeal would restore that bank-subsidized channel at federal expense.
The law required drug makers to discount medicines for Medicare beneficiaries caught in the coverage gap; repeal would lift that requirement, returning those costs to seniors.
